definition: Covert propaganda refers to media materials prepared by a government agency and then disseminated by a nongovernmental media outlet with the governmental source undisclosed [1]. Covert propaganda materials are “misleading as to their origin”[2]. However, the source must be intentionally misleading, and not just due to administrative carelessness. The term is in reference to a section in most federal omnibus appropriations bills stating: “No part of any appropriation contained in this Act shall be used for publicity or propaganda purposes not authorized by the Congress.” While not defined in legislation, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) oversees and investigates suspected violations. The GAO separates publicity or propaganda into three types of inappropriate activity: self-aggrandizement, purely partisan purposes, and covert propaganda. In order for materials to be considered covert propaganda, the disseminating governmental agency in question must desire that its authorship be obscured, and it must take steps to ensure that obscurity. “A critical element of covert propaganda,” reads a Government Accountability Office opinion, “is the concealment of the agency's role in sponsoring such material” [3]. The prohibition also applies to communications prepared by private contractors at the behest of a government agency [4]. Covert propaganda does not include messages and materials published by government whistleblowers [5]. covered option / covert propaganda Dictionary compilation | 26 September 2026 Examples of non-covert propaganda: The GAO has expressed deference to agency materials that might be seen as covert. For example, Federal Trade Commission material advocating for Postal Service deregulation, in which the agency was clearly identified as the producer, was deemed not covert propaganda [6]. Advertisements produced and disseminated by the Department of Health and Human Services in support of the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003 were not covert propaganda because they identified HHS as the source [7].
